To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
hypoxia and VECG-Axxxa isoform expression is dysregulated in IPF and that this dysregulation may be a driver of fibrosis.
hypoxia, but not hyperoxia, induces VEGF-A protein expression in IPF fibroblasts and that VEGF-A expression and VEGF receptor expression are differentially regulated by hypoxia in IPF fibrosis.
VEGF-A and its receptors are dysregulated in hypoxia and/or hyperoxia, and that VEGF-A may be a key driver of fibrogenesis and fibrotic lung diseases.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of hypoxia on the expression of the VEGF-A gene family in normal and IPF fibroblasts.
the role of hypoxaemia and hyperoxia, as well as VEGF-A, on the development and progression in IPF.
the effects of hypoxia on the expression of VEGFs and their receptors in normal and diseased lung tissue.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
hypoxia and hypoxia mimetics are not a good idea in the treatment of IPF.
the effects of hypoxia on VEGF-A expression are mediated via HIF-1alpha, and that the effects of hyperoxia are mediated via the VEGF-A/VEGF-R2/PI3K/Akt pathway.
the VEGF-A system is dysregulated by hypoxaemia and hyperoxia, with a differential effect on expression of the VEGF isoforms and receptors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
VEGF-A and VEGF-Rs are dysregulated in IPF and that hypoxia and VVEGFR2 may be involved in IPF pathogenesis.
hypoxia and VVEGF-Axxxa isoform expression are upregulated in the fibroblasts of IPF and may contribute to the development of lung fibrosis.
the differential expression of hypoxia/hyperoxia regulated VEGF-A and VEGF receptors in IPF may contribute to the development of fibrosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
hypoxia is a driver of fibrogenesis and VEGF-xxxa isoform is a potential target for treatment of IPF.
the differential expression of isoforms and VEGF receptors in response to hypoxia and/or hyperoxia may be an underlying mechanism of fibrosis.
VEGF-A and VEGF receptor expression is differentially regulated by hypoxia/hyperoxia in normal and fibrotic lung fibroblasts and that this differential regulation may be a driver of fibrosis.
